items.stem: Complete the statement: Gross margin is calculated as …
items.answer: gross profit ÷ revenue × 100
items.markingKey: gross profit ÷ revenue × 100. On selling price [1]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why a business's gross margin might fall.
items.answer: Selling prices cut to meet competition; purchase costs rose but could not be passed on; change in sales mix toward lower-margin goods; theft or wastage of inventory.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the gross margin and the profit margin.
items.answer: Gross margin compares gross profit (after cost of sales) with revenue; profit margin compares profit after all expenses with revenue, showing control of overheads too.
items.markingKey: Gross – after COS [1]; profit margin – after expenses [1] [2]

items.stem: Complete the statement: ROCE is calculated as …
items.answer: profit from operations ÷ capital employed × 100
items.markingKey: profit from operations ÷ capital employed × 100. Profit before interest and tax [1]

items.stem: Explain why ROCE is regarded as a key measure of performance.
items.answer: It relates the profit made to all the long-term capital used to make it, so businesses of different sizes can be compared and the return compared with alternatives.
items.markingKey: Profit relative to capital [1]; comparability/alternative returns [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain one limitation of ROCE.
items.answer: Capital employed is based on book values (historical cost, depreciation), so older assets give a higher ROCE; year-end figures may not be representative.

items.stem: Explain why expense-to-revenue ratios are more useful than the money amounts of expenses.
items.answer: They allow comparison over time and with other firms of different sizes, showing whether costs are controlled relative to activity.

items.stem: Explain how gross margin, expenses to revenue and profit margin are linked.
items.answer: Profit margin = gross margin − total expenses as a % of revenue, so any change in profit margin is explained by the other two.
